title: How World War II Happened — Minute by Minute
sources: Wikipedia, Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bombings_of_Hiroshima_and_Nagasaki

beats.say: New York, 1944. A young Englishman in his early thirties is about to put on the uniform of the United States Navy.
He has asked the President himself for permission. His name is William Patrick Hitler.
His uncle is Adolf Hitler. The dictator of Germany. The man America is at war with.
The nephew was born in Liverpool. He worked in his uncle's Germany for years. His uncle reportedly called him, my loathsome nephew.
Now he wants to fight his own family. This is the Second World War, from 1939 to 1945, told from both sides.
Germany and Japan on one side. Britain, the Soviet Union and America on the other.
It is the deadliest war in human history. Somewhere between seventy and eighty-five million people die.
We will follow it minute by minute. The decisions in palaces and bunkers. The people on the beaches, in the cities and under the bombs.
And through it all, we follow one family. An uncle who started a war in Europe. And a nephew who crossed an ocean to fight him.
How does Hitler's own nephew end up in the American Navy? And what happens to him when the war is over?
To answer that, we have to start in Liverpool, in a boarding house, in 1911.

chapters.title: Before World War Two: A Boy From Liverpool

beats.say: Dublin, 1909. A horse show. A young Irish woman named Bridget Dowling is there with her father, William.
She meets a charming Austrian. He says he is a wealthy hotelier. His name is Alois Hitler.
Alois left his own home in Austria at fourteen, after a violent row with his father. He has been on the move ever since, and he is good at telling stories.
He is not wealthy. He is a poor kitchen porter at the Shelbourne Hotel. And he has already been to prison twice, for theft.

card.note: Alois Hitler Jr., prison terms for theft

talk.text: The Irish girl thinks you own this hotel.

beats.say: Her father does not approve. So on the third of June, 1910, the couple elope to London and marry.
They settle in Liverpool, at a boarding house in Toxteth. Number one hundred and two, Upper Stanhope Street.
On the twelfth of March, 1911, their only child is born. They name him William Patrick.
Alois has a half-brother back in Austria, from his father's later marriage. His name is Adolf. Nobody in Liverpool has ever heard of him.
Alois tries a restaurant on Dale Street. Then a boarding house. Then a hotel. Every one of them fails.
Years later, Bridget writes a memoir. She claims that Adolf himself came to stay with them in Liverpool, from November 1912 to April 1913.
Historians are not convinced. One of them, Peter Longerich, says there is hardly any reliable evidence about Hitler's life in those years. The question is still open.
But not all of them dismiss it. The Canadian historian Alan Cassels wrote, I'm inclined to believe his sister-in-law. Did the future dictator once live in Liverpool? Nobody can prove it either way.

card.text: I'm inclined to believe his sister-in-law.

beats.say: What is certain is this. In May 1914, Alois leaves for Germany, alone. He says he is going to start a restaurant business.
That summer, the First World War breaks out. He does not come back.
In Germany, he marries again, in 1916, without a divorce. Back in Liverpool, Bridget raises William on her own.
In 1920, his new German wife gives birth to a son, Heinz. So William now has a half-brother in Germany he has never met.
In 1924, the German courts charge Alois with bigamy. He escapes conviction, partly because Bridget speaks up for him. She agrees to a separation, and later a divorce.
So the boy grows up English, with a German surname that means nothing to anyone. Yet.
In 1929, his father asks to see him. William is eighteen. His mother agrees, and he travels to Germany. Four years later, the family name will mean everything.
Berlin, the thirtieth of January, 1933. The old president, Paul von Hindenburg, appoints a new chancellor.
Adolf Hitler, leader of the Nazi Party, is now head of the German government.
Conservative politicians talked the old president into it. They think they can control Hitler. They are wrong.
By August 1934, Hitler has a new title. Führer. The leader.
Many Germans cheer him. Many others fear him. Very soon, it becomes dangerous to say so out loud.
That same year, 1933, William Patrick Hitler arrives in Berlin. His mother has encouraged him to go.
He is twenty-two years old, and the nephew of the most powerful man in Germany. Surely that opens doors.
His father is already in Germany too. Alois Junior joined his half-brother's Nazi Party back in 1926, and left it again a year later. He runs a restaurant, and keeps out of politics.
It does, a little. His uncle finds him a job, at the Reichsbank, Germany's central bank, in Berlin. He will work there for most of the 1930s.
Later he sells cars for Opel. Then he is fired. The police claim he is selling cars using the Hitler name.
[chuckle] Of all the names in Germany to sell cars with, that one was always going to be noticed.
Then, the story goes, William makes a threat. He says he could tell the press a rumour about the family.
The rumour is about who Hitler's grandfather really was. Nothing is ever proved. But William's salary is suddenly doubled.
Then his uncle makes him an offer. Give up British citizenship, and take a high-ranking job.

talk.text: Give up the British passport. A fine job awaits.

beats.say: William smells a trap. If he stops being British, nobody can protect him. So he says no.
It is a strange position. He is the Führer's nephew, living in Berlin, with a British passport in his pocket. And his uncle does not seem to like him at all.
And outside the bank, his uncle's Germany is getting ready for something much bigger than a family argument.
Munich, the thirtieth of September, 1938. It is about half past one in the morning.
Four men have just signed an agreement. Hitler of Germany. Mussolini of Italy. Chamberlain of Britain. Daladier of France.
It hands Germany the Sudetenland, a mountain region of Czechoslovakia. About three million people live there, most of them ethnic Germans.
One country is missing from the room. Czechoslovakia itself. They were not invited to the conference.
Now the other side. For Britain and France, the last world war ended only twenty years ago. Nobody wants another one.
That day, Neville Chamberlain flies back to Britain, and holds up a sheet of paper with Hitler's signature on it.

scene.caption: Chamberlain with the Anglo-German declaration, 30 September 1938

beats.say: He tells the crowds in London it means peace for our time.
From the tenth of October, German troops take over the Sudetenland.
Then, in March 1939, Hitler breaks his promise. Germany takes the rest of the Czech lands.
The peace for our time has lasted less than six months.
In Berlin, William Patrick Hitler reads the signs. In 1939 he leaves Germany for good, and returns to England.
He tells The Times newspaper about his uncle. I believe he has created a Frankenstein which even he perhaps cannot stop.

lines: William Patrick Hitler on his uncle:

talk.text: Your uncle. What is he like?
I believe he has created a Frankenstein which even he perhaps cannot stop.

beats.say: He writes an article for the American magazine Look. The title is, Why I Hate My Uncle.
And an American newspaper owner, William Randolph Hearst, brings him and his mother to America. For a lecture tour.
Mother and son cross the Atlantic. They expect to go home again. They never will.
Moscow, late August 1939. Two enemies sign a deal that shocks the world.
Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union promise not to attack each other. It is signed by the two foreign ministers, Ribbentrop and Molotov.

lines: agree not to attack each other

beats.say: Hitler no longer fears a war on two fronts. And Poland now sits between two dictators.
The night of the thirty-first of August. A German radio station near Gleiwitz, on the Polish border, is attacked.
The attackers are dressed like Polish soldiers. They are German units in disguise. Germany now has its excuse.
The first of September, 1939. Hitler has ordered the fighting to start at four forty-five in the morning.
In the harbour at Danzig, the old German battleship Schleswig-Holstein opens fire on the Polish depot at Westerplatte.
Across the border come sixty-six German divisions, two thousand seven hundred and fifty tanks, and over two thousand aircraft.
Two thousand seven hundred and fifty tanks against two hundred and ten. Thirteen German tanks for every Polish one.

scene.place: GERMAN TANKS FOR EACH POLISH TANK

beats.say: Now the other side. Poland has about a million soldiers. But only two hundred and ten tanks.
And Poland is not even fully ready. Of the more than one point three million men it planned to call up, only about nine hundred thousand have answered the first order.
The Poles fight anyway. They are waiting for Britain and France to keep their promise.
Two days later, Britain and France declare war on Germany. The Second World War has begun.
On the seventeenth of September, the Soviet Union invades Poland from the east.
The Red Army brings more than four thousand seven hundred tanks of its own. Poland is now fighting on two fronts at once.
Caught between two armies, Poland falls. The last Polish units stop fighting on the sixth of October.
About sixty-six thousand Polish soldiers are dead, and close to seven hundred thousand are prisoners. Germany loses over sixteen thousand killed.
Behind the army come special units. Around fifty thousand Polish and Polish Jewish leaders and intellectuals are arrested or killed.
And in America, William Patrick Hitler hears the news. He and his mother are stranded. The war has closed the road home.

chapters.title: Dunkirk and the Battle of Britain

beats.say: The tenth of May, 1940. After months of quiet, Germany strikes west, into the Netherlands, Belgium and France.
German tanks race to the sea. British troops and many French soldiers are trapped around the port of Dunkirk.
On the twenty-fifth of May, the British War Office makes a painful decision. Its army will leave France, by sea, if it can.
Then, on the twenty-fourth of May, Hitler orders his tanks to halt. For three days, they wait.
Historians still argue about why. But for the men on the beaches, those three days are everything. The order is only lifted on the evening of the twenty-sixth.
Britain sends destroyers, ferries, fishing boats and pleasure boats across the Channel.

talk.text: A pleasure boat? To a war?

beats.say: In nine days, three hundred and thirty-eight thousand men are carried to Britain. Nearly a hundred and forty thousand of them are French, Polish and Belgian.

scene.caption: Troops from Dunkirk arriving at Dover, 31 May 1940

beats.say: Three hundred and thirty-eight thousand men in nine days. About thirty-seven thousand every single day.
Of the eight hundred and sixty-one vessels used, two hundred and forty-three are sunk.
On the fourteenth of June, German troops march into Paris.
On the twenty-second, France agrees to an armistice, at Compiègne.
Now Britain stands without France. For Hitler, the next battlefield is the sky.
And remember William Patrick Hitler? He is in America now, telling audiences who his uncle really is. But he is a speaker, not a soldier. Not yet.

talk.text: Is it true? You are really his nephew?

beats.say: From the tenth of July, the German air force, the Luftwaffe, fights the Royal Air Force over southern England.
If the Luftwaffe wins the sky, Germany can invade. If it loses, there can be no invasion.

talk.text: Too many. Up again in an hour.

beats.say: From the seventh of September, the bombs fall on London itself. The Blitz goes on until May 1941.

scene.caption: St Paul's Cathedral in the Blitz

beats.say: Now the other side. The young German airmen are a long way from home, over enemy country. Over nine hundred of them are shot down and captured.

talk.text: We are a long way from home.

beats.say: By the end, nearly two thousand German aircraft are destroyed, and over seventeen hundred British ones.
Over twenty-three thousand British civilians are killed in the battle. Both air forces lose thousands of aircrew.
The Luftwaffe never wins the sky. Hitler puts off the invasion, and in the end gives it up. So he turns east.
Sunday, the twenty-second of June, 1941. Hitler breaks his deal with the Soviet Union.
More than three point eight million Axis troops cross the border, along a front of about two thousand nine hundred kilometres.
The Soviet Union has millions of soldiers of its own, and around eleven thousand tanks. But it is caught off guard.
German armies drive deeper and deeper. Smolensk falls in late July.
On the second of October, the drive on Moscow begins.
And that is when the weather starts to matter.
Now the other side. For Soviet soldiers and families, this is not a war for borders. It is a fight for survival.

talk.text: Then this is where we stop them.

beats.say: Autumn rain turns the roads to mud. Then the snow comes.
By the fifth of December, the German offensive stalls at the edge of Moscow. That same day, the Red Army strikes back.
By German Army reports, over a hundred and eighty-six thousand Germans have been killed by the end of the year.
The machines are lost too. By the end of 1941, the Germans have lost over two thousand seven hundred tanks. The Soviets, over twenty thousand.
The Soviets have lost over half a million killed in action, and more than two million missing or captured.

card.note: Operation Barbarossa, to the end of 1941

beats.say: In just under six months, German forces have taken about one point six million square kilometres of Soviet land. But not Moscow. And not the war.
Over the whole war in the east, the Axis will capture about five million Red Army soldiers. Millions of them will never come home.
In America, William Patrick Hitler watches from far away. He wants to fight his uncle. But America is still not at war.
That is about to change. In a single morning. On the other side of the world.

chapters.title: A Date Which Will Live in Infamy

beats.say: To understand that morning, go back to Japan's side of the story. July 1937, near Beijing.
A Japanese soldier, Private Shimura Kikujiro, goes missing near the Marco Polo Bridge.
Japanese troops demand to search the town of Wanping. The Chinese refuse. Shots are fired.
Private Shimura turns up safe. He had got lost. But the shooting does not stop. It becomes a full-scale war between Japan and China.
China will lose between fourteen and twenty million people in this war.
Japan's leaders want an empire in Asia. To fight for it, they need resources. Above all, oil.
In July 1941, Japan seizes French Indochina. The United States answers by stopping oil exports.
Now the other side. To Tokyo, the choice looks stark. Give up, or seize the oil of the Dutch East Indies by force.
To keep the American fleet from interfering, Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto plans a strike first.
Sunday, the seventh of December, 1941. Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. Seven forty-eight in the morning.
Three hundred and fifty-three Japanese aircraft, from six carriers, attack in two waves.
All eight American battleships in the harbour are damaged. Four are sunk. The USS Arizona will never sail again.
The strike force is led by Admiral Chuichi Nagumo. His six carriers have crossed the Pacific in secret to get here.
More than a hundred and eighty American aircraft are destroyed.
Two thousand four hundred and three Americans are killed. Japan loses twenty-nine aircraft.
Among the dead are two thousand and eight sailors, a hundred and nine Marines and two hundred and eighteen soldiers. Another eleven hundred and seventy-eight are wounded.
On the Japanese side, a hundred and twenty-nine men die. One sailor, from a midget submarine, is captured. The rest of the strike force sails home.
President Roosevelt calls it a date which will live in infamy. On the eighth of December, America declares war on Japan.

card.text: ...a date which will live in infamy.

talk.text: A date which will live in infamy.

beats.say: Three days later, Germany declares war on the United States. Now the nephew's new country is at war with his uncle.

chapters.title: The Nephew Writes to the President

beats.say: Now William Patrick Hitler has one goal. To join the fight against his uncle.
There is one small problem. [chuckle] His surname.
He is a British subject, living in America, called Hitler. Nobody quite knows what to do with a volunteer like that.
So he goes straight to the top. He writes to the President of the United States.
In short, he tells Roosevelt who he is, Hitler's nephew, and asks to be allowed to fight against his uncle.
A letter to the President, from a man called Hitler, asking to fight. [chuckle] It is not the kind of letter that gets a quick yes.

talk.text: A letter for the President. From a Mr... Hitler.
Put it on the pile. The big pile.

beats.say: His request has to go up through Washington. It will take a long time to be answered.
Meanwhile, in early 1942, the Nazi leadership decides to murder every Jew in Europe. They call it the Final Solution.
Extermination camps such as Auschwitz-Birkenau become the centre of the killing.
By the end of the war, around six million Jews have been murdered. About two out of every three Jews in Europe.
There is no other side to this. Only the people who did it, and the people it was done to.
June 1942, the middle of the Pacific. Japan plans to lure the American carriers into a trap at Midway Atoll.
But American codebreakers have partly broken the Japanese naval code. They know the target is called AF. They don't know where AF is.
So Midway sends out a fake report, in plain language. Its water plant has broken down. Soon a Japanese message says AF is short of water.
From the fourth to the seventh of June, American planes sink four Japanese carriers. Akagi, Kaga, Soryu and Hiryu.

scene.caption: Dauntless bombers over the burning Mikuma, 6 June 1942

beats.say: About three thousand Japanese die, many of them experienced pilots. America loses the carrier Yorktown and about three hundred men. Japan will never replace what it lost.
The twenty-third of August, 1942. On the Volga River, the German Sixth Army attacks the city of Stalingrad.
The city carries Stalin's own name. For both dictators, it becomes a question of pride.
The fighting goes street by street. House by house. Floor by floor.
Then, on the nineteenth of November, the Red Army launches Operation Uranus.
The long flanks of the German Sixth Army run out across the open steppe. And they are held not by Germans, but by Germany's allies.
It smashes the Romanian armies guarding the Sixth Army's flanks. And the Sixth Army is surrounded.
Now the other side. Inside the ring, German soldiers run out of food and ammunition, in the Russian winter.
On the second of February, 1943, what is left of the Sixth Army surrenders.
About two hundred and thirty-five thousand Axis soldiers are taken prisoner.
Now the Soviet side. By one Russian count, the Red Army loses more than one point one million men at Stalingrad, killed, wounded, missing or captured.
On the Axis side, about half a million are dead.
Estimates of the casualties at Stalingrad run from eight hundred thousand to one and a half million.
It is one of the bloodiest battles ever fought. And from now on, in the east, Germany is going backwards.
In July 1943, the Allies land in Italy.
And in New York, William Patrick Hitler is still waiting for an answer.
1944. The answer finally comes. William Patrick Hitler is approved to join the United States Navy.
It has taken a special request to the President of the United States.
He doesn't carry a rifle. He becomes a pharmacist's mate, what the Navy later calls a hospital corpsman.
His job is to care for the sick and the wounded.
Think about it. The nephew of the man who started the war in Europe, now patching up the men who fight it.
He is wounded in action himself. He is awarded the Purple Heart.
Somewhere, a sailor is being bandaged by a man whose name tag says Hitler. We don't know what those patients said. But we can guess what they thought.
Remember the question we started with. How does Hitler's own nephew end up in the American Navy? The answer is simple. He kept asking until they said yes.
His uncle, meanwhile, has bigger worries. The Allies are about to land in France.
Southern England, early June 1944. General Eisenhower has picked the fifth of June to invade France.
But on the fourth, there are high winds, heavy seas and low cloud.
His weatherman, Group Captain James Stagg, predicts a short break in the weather.

talk.text: A short break in the weather. On the sixth.
Then we go on the sixth.

beats.say: If they wait, the next good tides will not come until about the eighteenth of June. So Eisenhower decides. They go on the sixth.
Shortly after midnight, about twenty-four thousand American, British and Canadian airborne troops land behind the coast.
Around six thirty in the morning, the landings begin. Five beaches. Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword.
Americans at Utah and Omaha. British at Gold and Sword. Canadians at Juno.
About five thousand ships. And a hundred and fifty-six thousand soldiers land that day.
A hundred and fifty-six thousand soldiers in one day. About sixty-five hundred every hour.
Now the other side. The German air force can put only eight hundred and fifteen aircraft over Normandy. The Allies have more than nine thousand.
By nightfall, at least ten thousand Allied soldiers are casualties. Four thousand four hundred and fourteen are confirmed dead.
German losses that day are estimated at between four and nine thousand men.
Offshore, almost two hundred thousand sailors keep the ships, the shells and the supplies coming.
Now Germany is caught between two fronts. The Soviets in the east. And the Allies in the west.
April 1945. Berlin. The Red Army is fighting its way into the city.
Hitler is underground, in a concrete shelter in the centre of Berlin. The Führerbunker.
Shortly after midnight on the twenty-ninth of April, he marries Eva Braun, in a small civil ceremony, in a map room.
By late morning on the thirtieth, Soviet troops are less than five hundred metres away.

scene.caption: The Soviet flag over the Reichstag, 1945

beats.say: That afternoon, at about half past three, Hitler shoots himself. Eva Braun takes cyanide.
For years afterwards, rumours say he escaped. The historian Anton Joachimsthaler, who studied the court findings, puts it plainly. There can no longer be the slightest doubt.

lines: the slightest doubt that on 30 April 1945
Adolf Hitler put an end to his life."

beats.say: On the first of May, German radio announces that Hitler is dead.
On the seventh of May, at two forty-one in the morning, in Reims in France, General Alfred Jodl signs Germany's surrender.
The Soviets object. They want the surrender signed in Berlin. So it is signed again there, dated the eighth of May.
In Berlin, at Karlshorst, Field Marshal Wilhelm Keitel signs for Germany. By then it is already past midnight.
So the West celebrates victory in Europe on the eighth. In Moscow it is already past midnight, so the Soviet Union celebrates on the ninth.

talk.text: Not here. Not until after midnight.

beats.say: And William's father? The British arrest Alois Hitler in 1945. They find he was never a member of the Nazi Party while his half-brother ruled. He had kept away from politics.
The uncle is dead. The nephew is alive, in an American uniform. But the war is not over. Not in the Pacific.
The sixth of August, 1945. Hiroshima, Japan. An American bomber drops a single bomb, called Little Boy.
Little Boy is a uranium bomb. The second bomb, three days later, will use plutonium. Hiroshima is a city of soldiers, workers, children and families.
By the end of the year, an estimated ninety thousand to a hundred and sixty-six thousand people in Hiroshima are dead.
Three days later, on the ninth of August, a second bomb, Fat Man, falls on Nagasaki. Sixty to eighty thousand more people die there.
At the same time, the Soviet Union declares war on Japan, and invades Manchuria.
In Tokyo, the emperor, Hirohito, records a message to his people. Japan will surrender.
But on the night of the fourteenth of August, army officers and soldiers raid the Imperial Palace. They want to destroy the recording.
Now the other side of that night. These officers want to fight on. Some reports say as many as a thousand of them take part.
They can't find it. It is hidden among documents in a small office. Palace staff smuggle out the records, one in a lunch bag.
Noon, the fifteenth of August. Many ordinary Japanese hear their emperor's voice for the first time.
It is not even live. It is a phonograph record. And it is the emperor's first ever radio address.
He says the war has developed, quote, not necessarily to Japan's advantage.
In the early hours, rebels led by Major Kenji Hatanaka even try to stop the broadcast at the radio station. The army orders them to stand down.
He speaks of a new and most cruel bomb. And he asks his people to endure the unendurable.
The whole speech lasts about four and a half minutes. It ends a war that has lasted, for Japan and China, eight years.
On the second of September, 1945, Mamoru Shigemitsu signs the instrument of surrender for Japan.
The Second World War is over. Six years and one day after it began.
Count the dead side by side. The Soviet Union, around twenty-six million. China, fourteen to twenty million.
Germany, around seven million. Poland, about six million. Japan, up to three million.
The Japanese government itself puts its war dead at three point one million.
Britain, about four hundred and fifty thousand. The United States, about four hundred and twenty thousand.
Most of the dead are not soldiers. They are civilians.
Poland loses about one in every six of its people. The Soviet Union, nearly one in seven. Britain, less than one in a hundred.
About three in every hundred people alive in 1940 are gone. Around half of them are killed directly by the fighting, the bombs and the camps. The rest die of hunger and disease.
And William Patrick Hitler? In 1947, he leaves the Navy.
That same year he marries Phyllis Jean-Jacques. And he changes his name. To Stuart-Houston.
He settles in Patchogue, on Long Island, New York. From his house on Silver Street, he runs a small business testing blood samples.
He calls it Brookhaven Laboratories. It has nothing to do with the famous national laboratory of the same name. It is run from a house, at seventy-one Silver Street.
He and Phyllis have four sons. The first, born in 1949, is named Alexander Adolf. Even after everything, the name Adolf stays in the family.
His mother, Bridget, lives on Long Island too, until she dies in November 1969, aged seventy-eight.
Across the Atlantic, his father Alois dies in Hamburg in 1956. By then he has a different name too. Alois Hiller.
William Patrick Stuart-Houston dies in Patchogue on the fourteenth of July, 1987. He is seventy-six.
He is buried at Holy Sepulchre Cemetery, in the same cemetery as his mother.
His uncle left behind a continent of ruins and graves. The nephew left behind a quiet house, a medal, and four sons with a different name.
He never chose the name he was born with. What he chose was the side he fought on.

outro.text: Every border has two sides, and so does every family. This one had the man who started a war in Europe, and the boy from Liverpool who joined the other side.
outro.question: If your surname had been Hitler in 1942, would you have changed it, or kept it and fought?

hook: In 1944, Adolf Hitler's British-born nephew joined the United States Navy to fight his uncle. This is the Second World War, from both sides.
about: World War Two from 1939 to 1945, told from both sides and minute by minute, through William Patrick Hitler: the Liverpool boy whose uncle became Germany's dictator. Munich and 'peace for our time', 4:45 am in Poland, Dunkirk and the Battle of Britain, Operation Barbarossa, the Marco Polo Bridge and Pearl Harbor, the Holocaust, Midway, Stalingrad, D-Day, the bunker in Berlin, Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the emperor's broadcast, and what happened to the nephew who changed his name.
